brief.head: Best minds behind bars
brief.text: There were pe­ri­ods, Amit Varma said, when a country’s finest in­tel­lec­tu­als were not in uni­ver­si­ties, think tanks or air-conditioned cafes. “They were in jails.” {023-C03}

brief.head: Left, right, same game
brief.text: Labels like left and right hide[[x3]] what is re­ally going on, Ajay Shah ar­gued. Populism ig­nites ha­tred against elites, and who­ever wields it, “at heart, it’s the same.” {023-C07}

brief.head: Chicken for the guest
brief.text: In Pashtun vil­lages, Mukulika Banerjee found[[x5]][[x4]], beef was the sta­ple, but every house­hold kept an ex­pen­sive chicken for hon­oured guests. To spare her hosts, she ate beef. {023-S04}

brief.head: The looking-glass self
brief.text: Amit Varma’s un­writ­ten novel *Missing* has a stu­dent van­ish from his hos­tel, and in a par­al­lel strand ev­ery­one else van­ishes. “If other peo­ple van­ish, what is the self?” {023-C10}[[x6]]

brief.head: Sorry, Govindji
brief.text: Govind Nihalani once wanted to film[[x7]] Amit Varma’s novel *My Friend Sancho*. When it stalled, an em­bar­rassed Varma stopped meet­ing him. On air, he apol­o­gised. {023-S17}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah play producer for a day
lead.head: Seven stories in want of a studio

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 23

body: Ajay Shah came out of Christopher Nolan’s *Dunkirk* feel­ing that a time ma­chine had taken him back to 1940. {#dunkirk}
Why stop there, he asked. So many other scenes from his­tory linger in the imag­i­na­tion that he and Amit Varma de­cided to hand a few to the peo­ple who make films.
The re­sult was seven pitches for films and web se­ries[[x2]][[x1]]: four from Varma, three from Shah, with nei­ther know­ing the other’s list in ad­vance.
The sto­ries, Varma said, “also re­veal a bit about us and the things that we care about”.
Shah pre­dicted that Varma would one day be­come one of the world’s great movie mak­ers. “You left me speech­less for a mo­ment,” Varma replied.
## Heroes of a kind
Varma, in a red kurta to hon­our the Red Shirts, opened with Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the Pathan whose Khudai Khidmatgar met every provo­ca­tion with non­vi­o­lence.
Pakistan’s state crushed the move­ment after Partition. But when Bacha Khan died in 1988, a lonely old man, his mem­ory still meant some­thing to the com­mon peo­ple. {023-S01}

Shah’s reply was a raid. At the air­field of Tatsinskaya, Soviet tanks sat at the edge of the run­way and shot down the German trans­ports sup­ply­ing Stalingrad, one by one, as they took off. {023-S06}
Varma sug­gested that the real hero was some­where in a back room, a thinker like Shah, plan­ning the op­er­a­tion. “Of course,” Shah said, “no ques­tion.”
Varma’s sec­ond pitch was Haimabati Sen, mar­ried at nine to a wid­ower of 45, wid­owed at ten, who made her way to Benares and be­came a doc­tor. {023-S08}
Shah fol­lowed with a theme rather than a tale: the bridges over which re­treat­ing German armies had to squeeze, and the mil­i­tary po­lice­men who killed their own sol­diers to keep order.
## The state against the cit­i­zen
The long­est pitch was Varma’s web se­ries on the Emergency, drawn from Coomi Kapoor’s book. It is dan­ger­ous to for­get his­tory, he said, be­cause “it rhymes in dis­turb­ing ways”.

Its scenes would in­clude a Haryana vil­lage be­sieged by po­lice dur­ing the ster­il­i­sa­tion drive, an ac­tress jailed for her friend­ship with George Fernandes, and a head­line the gov­ern­ment could not stop: “Babu beats Bobby”.
Then a fic­tion. Varma’s *Missing* is a novel he once meant to write, about a stu­dent who van­ishes from his hos­tel, and about a world in which, for that stu­dent, ev­ery­one else has van­ished.
Shah re­vealed that his own parents’ elope­ment had once been op­tioned for a film.
## A title in wartime

Shah kept the last word for him­self, with the story of how Arthur Koestler’s *Darkness at Noon* was writ­ten in Paris as France fell, nearly lost, and named by its trans­la­tor, Daphne Hardy. {023-S20}
The book was re­ally in­flu­en­tial, Shah said. It changed the world, and in his telling it tipped the French elec­tion of 1946.
Varma closed by hop­ing some of the films would get made, so that the hosts could walk red car­pets. Then he turned to Shah. “You couldn’t even wear a red shirt.”

second.label: Pitching the Emergency
second.head: A blockbuster backfires
second.deck: How a Doordarshan screening of Bobby failed to keep a rally empty

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the day Babu beat Bobby

body: In 1977, as Amit Varma re­called it, the gov­ern­ment was wor­ried about a JP Narayan rally at which Jagjivan Ram was to speak. So it told Doordarshan to show *Bobby*, a huge hit of 1973, on the the­ory that ev­ery­one would stay home. {#bobby}
The rally was packed. Jagjivan Ram’s nick­name was Babu, and the next day’s head­line read “Babu beats Bobby”. {023-S14}

Varma would open his Emergency web se­ries here: a portly, ner­vous politi­cian putting on his cap back­stage, in­ter­cut with a fam­ily hud­dled around a 1970s tele­vi­sion set, watch­ing Dimple Kapadia. The head­line, he said, was the great­est in in­de­pen­dent India’s his­tory.

quote.text: And the head­line in the news­pa­per the next day was Babu beats Bobby.

third.head: Third time to Banaras

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his parents’ elopement

body: Amit Varma had just apol­o­gised on air for ghost­ing the film­maker Govind Nihalani when Ajay Shah men­tioned a pro­duc­tion agree­ment of his own: his parents’ story had once been op­tioned.

They had an inter-caste mar­riage, and they eloped three times. “The first two times were ter­ri­ble, vi­o­lent events,” Shah said, “and then they ran and ran and did not stop run­ning till they reached Banaras.” {023-S18}
There they mar­ried in se­cret, in an Arya Samaj cer­e­mony. The film was never made.

Varma wanted to dig into it a lit­tle more, and could not re­sist a dig of his own. “And out of that great ro­man­tic, coura­geous af­fair emerges a bor­ing card car­ry­ing econ­o­mist,” he said. “What a waste. What a waste.” {023-J06}

box.title: Servants of a higher God
box.text: Gandhi first saw in Bacha Khan[[x9]][[x8]] a kin­dred soul, then an in­spi­ra­tion, and once called his move­ment the prac­ti­cal form of the non­vi­o­lence he be­lieved in. Amit Varma reads its ‘God’ as a set of higher prin­ci­ples. {023-J14}

sections.label: Amit’s first
sections.head: Unarmed, and unafraid
sections.caption: the Servants of God
body: Amit Varma’s first pitch was a web se­ries in two strands. One fol­lows Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, known as Bacha Khan, whose Khudai Khidmatgar, the ‘ser­vants of God’, grew from a thou­sand mem­bers in 1930 to lakhs of marchers in red kur­tas. {#members}

The other fol­lows Mukulika Banerjee, a PhD stu­dent[[x11]][[x10]] in India in the late 1980s, who could not square his move­ment with aca­demic con­ven­tion. Peasants sup­pos­edly did not do mass pol­i­tics; Pathans were sup­pos­edly a vi­o­lent fron­tier peo­ple.
An ad­viser told her to do a PhD only if she had a ques­tion that kept her up at night. She had one. {023-S03}

For two years no­body would back a woman going to the North-West Frontier Province. When money came, partly from abroad, she learned Pashto, wore a chador and went from vil­lage to vil­lage look­ing for sur­vivors. The book, *The Pathan Unarmed*, took ten years.
## Rooted at home

Her an­swer, which Varma read out, was that Bacha Khan built non­vi­o­lence from what his peo­ple al­ready held: pa­tience in Islam, the greater jihad against one’s own fear and anger, and the Pashtun codes of courage, hos­pi­tal­ity and refuge. The British were un­wanted guests, to be evicted “po­litely but firmly”. {023-C01}
~ The Pakistani state later crushed the move­ment. Yet when Bacha Khan died in 1988, Varma said, the com­mon peo­ple still re­mem­bered. {023-S01}

quote.text: The state might have for­got­ten you and cast you away, but it still means some­thing to the com­mon peo­ple.

sections.label: Ajay’s first
sections.head: Hit them where they eat
sections.caption: the Soviet deep battle
body: Ajay Shah’s first pitch was set on the Eastern Front[[x12]], where about 250,000 German troops were en­cir­cled at Stalingrad. Under nor­mal con­di­tions they needed 700 to 900 tons of sup­plies a day. {#tons}

Hitler’s team tried to keep them alive by air, as the Germans had done a year ear­lier for about 100,000 men near Leningrad. The bare sur­vival min­i­mum was 300 tons a day. What ac­tu­ally got through was 100 to 150. {#airlift}
## Choke the sup­ply line

That made the air­fields the tar­get. Soviet doc­trine, Shah said, is not to hit the enemy head on but to work out its lo­gis­tics and hit those in­stead, the so-called deep bat­tle. Ukraine, he noted, is doing the same to the Russian in­vaders today. {023-C04}

He added a point peo­ple rarely con­sider. Planes must be light, so many parts are made to wear out quickly. “It’s one thing to own a plane,” he said. “It’s a dif­fer­ent thing for that plane to be air­wor­thy.” {023-C05}
~ The cor­rect level of human drama, Shah said, is *Dunkirk*’s: the events them­selves are the grand drama. Amit Varma, no Christopher Nolan fan­boy, called it the best war film ever made. {023-R16}

quote.text: You don’t hit the enemy, you fig­ure out their lo­gis­tics and you hit the lo­gis­tics. You choke the lo­gis­tics.

sections.label: Amit’s second
sections.head: A child widow’s long run
sections.caption: Haimabati Sen
body: Amit Varma’s sec­ond pitch opens in a sepia store­room. A woman’s hand un­latches an old trunk and lifts out yel­lowed, half-torn pa­pers. On a sec­ond sound­track, a child’s feet run, stum­ble and fall. Then the cred­its.

The pa­pers are the mem­oirs of Haimabati Sen, born in 1866 to a poor fam­ily in Khulna, then in Bengal and now in Bangladesh. At six, in the famine of 1872, she was caught steal­ing rice from the fam­ily store for the starv­ing poor out­side.
Her learn­ing alarmed her el­ders, and at nine she was mar­ried to a 45-year-old wid­ower with two chil­dren her own age. {#nine}

By twelve she was a des­ti­tute child widow, her money taken by an uncle. Many child wid­ows, Varma said, ended up in pros­ti­tu­tion. Haimabati went to Benares, ed­u­cated her­self and be­came a doc­tor. {023-S08}
## No path laid out
Varma first read about her in Kavitha Rao’s *Lady Doctors*. Every woman doc­tor of that cen­tury was re­mark­able, he said, be­cause a man could ar­rive by in­er­tia and a woman could not. {023-C11}
~ She began her mem­oirs in the 1920s and died in 1933. The pa­pers lay in a trunk for eighty years, until Tapan Raychaudhuri con­vinced the fam­ily that they were a big deal. {023-S09}

quote.text: Why is this not a web se­ries? Why is this not a film? What are you doing?

sections.label: Amit’s third
sections.head: The Emergency, in episodes
sections.caption: the Emergency
body: Amit Varma’s third pitch was a web se­ries on the Emergency, drawn from Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency: A Personal History*. Everyone should read it, he said, to un­der­stand the op­pres­sive power of the Indian state. {023-R11}
Its cast be­gins with Indira Gandhi. In a pri­vate let­ter to Sanjay in the late 1960s, which Kapoor re­pro­duces, she es­sen­tially says that they care only about power, not left or right. {023-S10}

Then the side char­ac­ters. Vidya Charan Shukla, as in­for­ma­tion and broad­cast­ing min­is­ter, told Delhi’s ed­i­tors: not one bad word against Indira Gandhi. Most com­plied. In LK Advani’s words, “when asked to bend, they chose to crawl[[x14]].” {023-S11}
## Lives, not sta­tis­tics

In Peepli, a Haryana vil­lage[[x13]], an age­ing wid­ower died dur­ing a forced ster­il­i­sa­tion. The vil­lage protested, po­lice laid siege, and at 6 AM two women mak­ing cow-dung cakes out­side were shot dead. {023-S12}

The ac­tress Snehalata Reddy’s crime was friend­ship with George Fernandes, then on the run. Denied treat­ment for her asthma in jail, she died of a heart at­tack shortly after her re­lease. {023-S13}

~ Many of today’s lead­ers were dis­senters then. Had he been one, Varma said, he would have vowed to treat the op­po­si­tion with dig­nity and let the press speak if he ever held power. He is not sure the les­son was learnt.

quote.text: The les­son I would take from this is how dan­ger­ous power is.

sections.label: Ajay’s last
sections.head: The book that swung France
sections.caption: the battle of ideas
body: Ajay Shah wanted his story to be the last word. It was about Arthur Koestler who, with George Orwell and Albert Camus, “lived at the dark cross­roads of lit­er­a­ture and pol­i­tics”, in Lionel Trilling’s words.
*Darkness at Noon*, Shah said, goes in­side the minds of the Soviet com­mu­nist lead­ers who con­fessed to grotesque crimes in court. {023-R17}

Written in Paris as the Germans ar­rived, it sur­vived by luck, and was ti­tled by its trans­la­tor, Daphne Hardy. Shah ar­gued that it tipped the French elec­tion of 1946, which the Communist Party lost. {#french}
## The bat­tle of ideas

Shah ranks Koestler and Orwell along­side Milton Friedman, Hayek and George Stigler in the 20th century’s bat­tle be­tween lib­eral democ­racy and au­thor­i­tar­ian and pop­ulist philoso­phies. Many peo­ple, he said, have still not in­ter­nalised its ba­sics. {023-C12}

In 2015 the German man­u­script turned up in Switzerland, and a new trans­la­tion fol­lowed, in­formed by the briefly opened Kremlin ar­chives. Shah held up his two most prized pos­ses­sions: a 1941 edi­tion that came from his fa­ther, and the 2015 one. {023-S21}
~ Amit Varma an­swered with Stefan Zweig’s *The World of Yesterday*, read­ing its lament that “all the pale horses of the apoc­a­lypse have stormed through my life”. {023-R18}

quote.text: Dear reader, I com­mend you please read these books, and you know what? Read both ver­sions.

portraits.caption: Arthur Koestler
portraits.credit: Eric Koch for Anefo, CC BY-SA 3.0

quote.text: India con­tains mul­ti­tudes. India con­tains the op­po­site val­ues. Our cul­ture can cater to the worst of our in­stincts, but it can also cater to the best of our in­stincts.

p3.title: Scenes to shoot
p3.deck: Four stories from the episode, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s Eastern Front epic, set on a single airfield
stories.head: Tanks at the edge of the runway
body: The air­field at Tatsinskaya was the clos­est to the ac­tion. About 200 German planes were based there, fly­ing sup­plies to the army trapped in­side Stalingrad, and Ajay Shah’s film would be set on its run­way.
Each trans­port car­ried about 2.5 tons on a sor­tie of an hour and a half: think Bombay to Delhi, or Bombay to Bhopal, Shah said. It un­loaded, took on wounded men and flew back, again and again.

Soviet in­tel­li­gence knew what the air­field was for, though it lay about 80 km in­side German-held ter­ri­tory. In an al­most sui­ci­dal op­er­a­tion, a group of tanks and sol­diers punched through the thin German lines and headed for it. The sur­prise was com­plete: the scouts raised the alarm only ten min­utes be­fore the T-34s ar­rived. {#ten}
Pandemonium fol­lowed. Planes with too lit­tle fuel tried to take off at once, and many crashed into each other, under ar­tillery and tank fire.

Then came what Shah called one of the most price­less frag­ments of the story. T-34s parked at the edge of the run­way, aimed, and waited. As each plane lifted off, a tank shell, fly­ing more or less straight, blew it up. “The tanks were like fat frogs grab­bing one drone ant at a time,” he said. {023-S06}
By Shah’s mem­ory, about 70 planes were de­stroyed and about 130 got away. {#seventy}
~ The sur­vivors had to fly from a far­ther air­field, mak­ing longer trips with fewer planes. The sup­ply of the Sixth Army was shat­tered. Weeks later, Paulus sur­ren­dered. {#paulus}
stories.why: Big things often hinge on lit­tle things, Amit Varma said, and this raid is at once a mi­cro­cosm and a macro­cosm of the war. The he­roes, the hosts agreed, are the plan­ners in a back room, work­ing out the lo­gis­tics.
stories.postscript: Varma pre­ferred this use of “fat frogs”. The last time Shah used the phrase, he said, it was to tell Varma to lose weight. {023-J05}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the raid on Tatsinskaya

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a scene that played out about ten times
stories.head: Shot by their own side
body: The Red Army cov­ered about 2,500 km from Stalingrad to Berlin in about 500 days, Ajay Shah said: the dis­tance from Ludhiana to Kanyakumari. {#berlin}

About ten times along the way, a re­treat­ing German army, with its men, equip­ment and stores, had to cross a river by a sin­gle bridge. Artillery was too im­pre­cise to de­stroy such bridges eas­ily, so they held. But every cross­ing was an op­er­a­tions prob­lem: what to leave be­hind, and how many ve­hi­cles of what kind could get across in a day.
Tired, scared men tended to break ranks, and a mob wrecks a cross­ing. At sev­eral of these cross­ings, the German mil­i­tary po­lice killed German sol­diers to hold the dis­ci­pline. {023-S07}
~ Shah reached for fluid me­chan­ics. “What you want is a lam­i­nar flow and not a tur­bu­lent flow,” he said. {023-C06}

quote.text: So think of each bridge as a choke point where there is a trapped army and its equip­ment and its stores.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the river crossings

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a stranger’s kindness in the Emergency
stories.head: A note falls from a van
body: During the Emergency, the jour­nal­ist Virendra Kapoor, Coomi Kapoor’s hus­band[[x15]], was moved be­tween jails in a po­lice van. He wanted her to know which sta­tion he would be at, Amit Varma said, so that she could see him.

He scrib­bled a parchi with her land­line num­ber and dropped it out of the back. A man on a scooter be­hind the van saw it fall, waited until the van was out of sight, picked it up and got the mes­sage to her. {#parchi}
She went to Bareilly to see him and three other pris­on­ers put on a train, not know­ing if she would see him again.
~ “And at the same time, and the scene is so cin­e­matic,” Varma said, a crowd at the other end of the plat­form was chant­ing slo­gans for a Congress politi­cian board­ing the same train. {023-S15}
stories.why: Under re­pres­sion, small acts of de­cency by strangers kept peo­ple con­nected. In the same frame, a few me­tres away, the pow­er­ful went on cel­e­brat­ing, which is what made the scene, to Varma, so cin­e­matic.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on a note dropped from a prison van

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a world-changing novel nearly vanished
stories.head: Page by page, as Paris fell
body: In 1940 Arthur Koestler, a Hungarian who wrote in German, was liv­ing in a dingy part of Paris with his girl­friend, Daphne Hardy, a 21-year-old British art stu­dent. He wrote *Darkness at Noon* page by page, Ajay Shah said, and she trans­lated each page into English.
Her German was not so good, and she knew lit­tle of Soviet Russia. So an in­ter­ro­ga­tion, in her English, be­came a hear­ing. {#interrogation}
Then the Germans reached Paris and France sur­ren­dered. Koestler, a wanted man, was in­terned. “The only rea­son he got away was be­cause of bad iden­tity in­fra­struc­ture,” Shah said. {023-S19}

~ Before they parted, he posted the German man­u­script to his ed­i­tor in Switzerland. Hardy hid the dan­ger­ous English one and was evac­u­ated from Marseille. Koestler es­caped, Shah thinks by walk­ing across the Pyrenees into Spain.
stories.why: A book that changed the world nearly never reached it. Its sur­vival hung on luck, on Hardy’s courage, and on German of­fi­cials who never worked out whom they had in­terned.
stories.postscript: Shah’s ad­vice to fans of dig­i­tal iden­tity: “Think twice.” {023-J10}

quiz.q: What did Mukulika Banerjee’s adviser say was the only reason to do a PhD?
quiz.a: A ques­tion that keeps you up at night, which you are des­per­ate to an­swer.

quiz.q: Why, by Ajay Shah’s account, did the airlift to Stalingrad collapse after the Tatsinskaya raid?
quiz.a: With about 70 planes lost, sur­vivors flew longer trips from a far­ther air­field.

quiz.q: What did the Akali prisoners do when British jailers ordered them to remove their turbans?
quiz.a: They stripped to their un­der­wear and kept only their tur­bans on.

quiz.q: What film did Doordarshan show to keep people away from Jagjivan Ram’s rally?
quiz.a: *Bobby*, the 1973 hit. The rally was packed any­way: Babu beats Bobby.

quiz.q: What fluid mechanics analogy did Ajay Shah use for an army crossing a bridge?
quiz.a: Laminar flow, not tur­bu­lent: a smooth, planned cross­ing, not a pan­ick­ing mob.

quiz.q: Who chose the title *Darkness at Noon*, and what had Koestler called his book?
quiz.a: Daphne Hardy, his trans­la­tor. His work­ing title was *Rubashov: A Novel*.

Pashtun code of of­fer­ing refuge to any­one, even an enemy.
Sterilisation, whose cer­tifi­cate some hos­pi­tals de­manded be­fore ad­mit­ting moth­ers.
A worker or vol­un­teer, such as the RSS man in Ahmedabad.
A loafer or rogue, which Varma claims to be.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 23. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Arthur Koestler (Eric Koch for Anefo, CC BY-SA 3.0); Abdul Ghaffar Khan (British India, public domain); Indira Gandhi (Prime Minister’s Office, GODL-India); Stefan Zweig (Franz Xaver Setzer (1886-1939), public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.creator: Mukulika Banerjee
shelf.why: Ten years of field­work on how Pathan peas­ants, stereo­typed as vi­o­lent, built the subcontinent’s great­est non­vi­o­lent move­ment, the Khudai Khidmatgar: Bacha Khan rooted it in the inner jihad and the Pashtun codes of courage, hos­pi­tal­ity and refuge.

shelf.title: The Incredible Curiosities of Mukulika Banerjee (Episode 276, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Mukulika Banerjee’s re­search sto­ries: her fight for fund­ing and her field­work in the North-West Frontier Province hunt­ing for sur­viv­ing Khudai Khidmatgars, which Amit calls a clas­sic quest nar­ra­tive.

shelf.title: My Life and Struggle
shelf.creator: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great au­to­bi­og­ra­phy.

shelf.title: Twilight in the Street of Storytellers
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A record of a place he loved be­fore he knew it had been the scene of a mas­sacre on the scale of Jallianwala Bagh.

shelf.title: Lady Doctors
shelf.creator: Kavitha Rao
shelf.why: He calls it a great book by an ex­cel­lent writer, about 19th-century women doc­tors who were all re­mark­able, be­cause a woman had to be re­mark­able even to be­come one.

shelf.title: Kavitha Rao and Our Lady Doctors (Episode 235, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The long-form con­ver­sa­tion be­hind the book that in­tro­duced him to Haimabati.

shelf.title: The Memoirs of Dr Haimabati Sen
shelf.creator: Geraldine Forbes and Tapan Raychaudhuri (editors)
shelf.why: It tells, in her own words, how a des­ti­tute child widow be­came a doc­tor.

shelf.title: Devangshu Datta Traded His Corduroy Pants (Episode 348, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A life-and-times con­ver­sa­tion with the hosts’ friend Devangshu Datta, from chess and his Brahmo Samaj back­ground to a fam­ily tree with three great-grandfathers who had in­sti­tu­tions named after them and a fourth who was a river pi­rate in Bengal.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mil­i­tary-strategy anal­y­sis of the war: how it is chang­ing the way wars are fought, Ukrainian in­no­va­tion, and its de­mo­graphic toll on Russia, from deaths to the flight of a mil­lion of its best and bright­est.

shelf.title: The Emergency: A Personal History
shelf.creator: Coomi Kapoor
shelf.why: A journalist’s first-hand ac­count of the Emergency, when half the op­po­si­tion and hordes of jour­nal­ists were jailed and a ster­il­i­sa­tion drive spun out of con­trol.

shelf.title: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with Coomi Kapoor, whose first-hand ac­count of the Emergency Amit re­lies on; a com­pan­ion to her book The Emergency: A Personal History.

shelf.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

shelf.title: The Looking-Glass Self
shelf.why: It frames the ques­tion of who we are once there is no one left to re­flect us back.

shelf.title: My Friend Sancho
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s own novel, which he dis­misses as slight (‘a bad novel I don’t talk about much’) while grant­ing that its premise was strong; it comes up in his story about Nihalani and Marathi cin­ema.

shelf.title: Dunkirk
shelf.creator: Christopher Nolan
shelf.why: Amit, no Nolan fan­boy, calls it the best war film ever made; Ajay, who knows the pe­riod deeply, sees it as the model for let­ting real events carry the drama.

shelf.title: Darkness at Noon
shelf.creator: Arthur Koestler
shelf.why: It goes in­side the minds of Soviet lead­ers con­fess­ing at show tri­als.

shelf.title: The World of Yesterday
shelf.creator: Stefan Zweig
shelf.why: Zweig’s mem­oir of liv­ing through Europe’s col­lapse into fas­cism, Bolshevism and na­tion­al­ism.

laughs.text: Ajay claims Amit will ‘be­come one of the world’s great movie mak­ers, and we’re ac­tu­ally giv­ing away some of his concepts’. Amit: ‘you left me speech­less for a moment’.
Ajay on the Bacha Khan pitch: ‘I will sign up to watch this web se­ries, even though I don’t have a Netflix sub­scrip­tion.’
Amit, of­fer­ing to be a showrun­ner: ‘why do you just want to be a card car­ry­ing econ­o­mist so bor­ing?’ Ajay: ‘I am a happy cus­tomer.’
Amit on Ajay call­ing the tanks fat frogs: ‘the last time you used that phrase fat frogs, you were ask­ing me to lose weight. So I’m hap­pier in this con­text.’
After hear­ing that Ajay’s par­ents eloped three times: ‘And out of that great ro­man­tic, coura­geous af­fair emerges a bor­ing card car­ry­ing econ­o­mist. What a waste. What a waste.’
On the ‘Babu Beats Bobby’ head­line, Amit: ‘it is just great­est fuck­ing head­line in in­de­pen­dent India’s his­tory.’

Ajay, Aadhaar-era pol­icy wonk, on Koestler es­cap­ing be­cause the Germans couldn’t iden­tify him: ‘So, gen­tle reader, if you ever think that dig­i­tal iden­tity is such a great thing. Think twice.’

Gandhi called Bacha Khan’s move­ment the prac­ti­cal form of the ide­al­is­tic non­vi­o­lence he be­lieved in. Amit says Bacha Khan’s ‘God’ in ‘ser­vants of God’ is best read as a set of higher prin­ci­ples.
L.K. Advani on the press dur­ing the Emergency: ‘when asked to bend, they chose to crawl.’ Simon Jenkins said he had seen Franco’s Spain and Mao’s China but never such a press crack­down.
Amit com­pares Vidya Charan Shukla to Gollum from ‘The Lord of the Rings’, en­slaved by his lust for power and end­ing up a piti­ful fig­ure.
Ajay quotes Lionel Trilling: Koestler, Orwell and Camus ‘lived at the dark cross­roads of lit­er­a­ture and politics’.
